This paper focuses on developing a musical instrument classification system that efficiently identifies instruments based on limited labeled data, utilizing a hierarchical hierarchical deep learning approach. We combine a hierarchical classification structure with a state-of-the-art feature extraction method, here Principal Component Analysis (PCA), to enhance performance. By reducing the complexity of the classification task through a hierarchical framework and applying PCA to extract key features, we achieve a robust and accurate instrument recognition system. Experiments conducted on a dataset containing 15 different musical instruments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, achieving a high accuracy of 98.5% in a two-level hierarchical classification task.

To enhance the effectiveness of AI systems in processing natural language, a novel dataset has been created, consisting of research articles on various topics including biology, physics, and computer science. Each article is accompanied by specific, targeted questions and corresponding answers, intended to guide AI models in deeply analyzing the content of scientific literature. A set of generic, pre-determined questions can serve as a valuable tool for evaluating the AI models' capability to accurately interpret technical content.

We've developed a high-precision computational method for pulsar timing array signal simulation that accounts for the merger phase in highly eccentric binary systems. This approach utilizes an advanced approximation, combining the $3.5$-PN point mass post-Newtonian expansion with the logarithmic phase correction proposed by Damour and Deruelle, over a vast parameter range. We've determined the $1$-sigma precision of this simulation method at $10^{-4}$, $10^{-3}$, $10^{-2}$, and $10^{-1}$ Hz for binary systems with frequencies of $0.1$, $0.3$, $1$, and $10$ Hz respectively. We've also determined the optimal eccentricity smoothing factor for various binary systems and determined the computational expense of this simulation method at around $10^9}$ floating-point operations per second. We've also created an efficient algorithm for real-time processing of pulsar timing array data and predict that this method will be capable of detecting merging eccentric binary systems through their persistent signals, even with future high-precision time stamps.

We introduce the ASEP velocity procedure, a concept where particles in asymmetric simple random walks gradually adjust their step sizes to achieve any given finite speed limit. This idea, developed over preceding research, builds on existing theories. Within the framework of macroscopic fluctuation theory, proof of existence and uniqueness for relevant density profiles can be established. Additionally, this concept may offer insights into queueing theory and self-organized criticality.

We examine mathematical models used to model infectious disease spread during epidemics and pandemics, with a focus on their application in the COVID-19 pandemic. Various modeling approaches are explored, and a review of key modeling concepts is presented. We examine major mathematical models used in infectious disease research, with a detailed analysis of a two-compartment model's role in understanding epidemic dynamics. We also examine how mathematical models can be applied to public health policy decisions during the COVID-19 pandemic.

This study examines linear Majorana particles, which possess the unique property of being their own antiparticles, along a specific direction in spacetime. While this behavior is not observed in conventional fermions, it is a natural property of massless particles like neutrinos and hypothetical axion-like particles. To better understand these particles, we have developed unbiased estimators for their statistical moments and moment-generating functions, which allow for the determination of the distribution of their polarizations. We have also derived the distribution of the angles between the directions in which these particles are helicity-pure. Notably, our research reveals that the directions of polarization for the same particle are uniformly and independently distributed. This property could be leveraged to establish a quantum version of the Bernoulli trial. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the directions of polarization for the same particle are maximally entangled in the sense of Merzbowm-Kirchball. To provide more insights, we have calculated the entanglement entropy, the entanglement concurrence, and the Tsallis-entropic concurrence.

Acronyms serve as effective word abbreviations that are extensively used in written English. Due to their frequent appearance in social media, they are difficult for NLP systems to process. To make NLP more efficient, a new acronym resolution tool called MadDog has been developed. MadDog is now being tested on platforms including Reddit and Twitter, where its effectiveness in providing immediate feedback to users who encounter unclear acronyms is being evaluated. A web interface for the system is now under development and feedback from a user study is being gathered to guide further improvements.

A theoretical model is proposed that describes an effective, bound pair of alkaline earth spinors in the singlet state, analogous to a molecular entity. The model is developed within a quantum field theory framework and incorporates Feshbach resonances induced by lasers. It is further demonstrated that, by adjusting quantum-induced scattering resonances, one can control the transition between molecular and dimer states through laser-induced three-body interactions.

DNA storage technology has been highly successful in managing vast amounts of data, and numerous optimization techniques have been proposed to enhance its performance and address key challenges in storage hierarchy and dynamic data updates. This paper introduces a new method for organizing storage systems based on hierarchical structures, and we developed HUDA, a unified framework that supports compression, hierarchy transformation, and data updates using DNA synthesis. Our research findings demonstrate that HUDA achieves exceptional compression rates, allowing for efficient storage of image and audio files using synthetic DNA, and it also maintains high-compression rates even after adding or deleting data. Furthermore, our results indicate that HUDA can effectively handle storage systems that require both high density and frequent hierarchy and information updates.

Topological properties of electronic and photonic crystals are primarily defined by point or line singularities in momentum space, where the energy gap closes. Recent breakthroughs have seen the implementation of 2D analogs of such singularities, known as nodal surfaces, in photonic crystals and other synthetic materials. These momentum-space features exhibit unique characteristics, facilitating topological state transfer between flat bands and offering robust connections between different materials. This paper provides an in-depth overview of nodal surfaces, highlighting their mathematical properties and potential for engineering topological states through surface and bulk mode couplings. It also outlines strategies for creating and manipulating 3D topological singularities and discusses the challenges and opportunities associated with hybrid systems featuring nodal surfaces.

A brain tumor is a malignant growth inside the cranial cavity that can affect both children and adults. It's a pressing health issue globally, ranking among the top five causes of death from cancer. Due to its complex nature, accurately diagnosing and identifying brain tumors is a significant challenge. Radiological imaging techniques, primarily MRI scans, are the standard for visualizing and assessing brain tumors. MRI scans employ magnetic fields and radio waves to create high-resolution images of the brain's internal structure. Nonetheless, MRI images often appear noisy and low in contrast, hindering radiologists' ability to clearly distinguish tumors from healthy brain tissue. To overcome this difficulty, researchers have turned to deep learning methods that can analyze imaging data and provide a reliable diagnosis. In this study, we present an innovative deep learning architecture called Multi-task focus directed network (MAG-Net) for simultaneously performing segmentation and classification of brain tumors using MRI scans. Our model employs an attention mechanism to prioritize relevant features and a multi-task learning framework to leverage the shared information between the two tasks. To evaluate its performance, we conducted experiments on three publicly available datasets, including the two versions of the Figshare and the LMIA datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that MAG-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Furthermore, our results indicate that the attention mechanism effectively highlights the relevant tumor regions and suppresses the noisy background, leading to more accurate diagnoses. A cutting-edge deep video deinterlacing system that processes active video streams is presented. Our key innovation is drawing on the characteristics of the video stream to identify and update relevant parts of a high-resolution video reconstruction, utilizing an efficient graph convolutional network for real-time processing. This model selectively incorporates high-resolution interlaced field data to replenish missing information in the reconstruction, allowing a high-resolution field to be analyzed on each video frame and achieving real-time performance. We obtain excellent results on public assessment datasets and are available to demonstrate our method using public video content. This work is selected for publication at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 2018.

In the study of nuclear physics, understanding the distribution of neutrons and protons within nuclei is essential. A key parameter that describes this distribution is the root-mean-square radius, which has been extensively analyzed for various nuclei across multiple frameworks. In a key development, an efficient framework was created to calculate the average square radius of neutron diffusion for specific nuclei. This framework employs a well-established relationship, deriving the neutron spread radius from the nuclear density distribution obtained from relativistic and non-relativistic mean field theory calculations. As a result, framework provides a straightforward and effective solution to obtaining neutron spread radius values, streamlining the process by bypassing the need for complex inverse problem-solving.

Precise and efficient hydrological forecasting relies heavily on the accuracy and speed of hydrological models, particularly those based on the shallow water equations. Traditionally, numerical methods like finite difference or finite volume are employed for solving these equations, but they often demand considerable computational time. In contrast, our research indicates that a deep learning-based approach using graph convolutional networks can significantly reduce computation time while maintaining high levels of accuracy. Specifically, our results show that this method retains 90% of the original accuracy while being 10 times faster than conventional numerical methods. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that a simplified graph-based approach retains 99% of the accuracy while being 100 times faster. These discoveries have significant hydrological and meteorological implications, particularly in the areas of flood warning systems and rapid weather forecasting.

High dynamic range photography demands multiple exposures across a scene. Conventional methods rely on pre-set exposure controls, yet there's a need for a more intuitive approach to determining the number and values of exposures. This paper presents a technique that utilizes a mobile camera to both automatically decide on exposure settings and combine images for high dynamic range photography. Firstly, we introduce a method to detect over- and under-exposed areas using a single camera based on analysis of the histogram and scene brightness. Building on this, we develop an optimization approach to expose to the maximum capability of the camera while preventing unnecessary multiple exposures. Finally, we present a method to decide whether to use a single, dual-layer or three-layer exposure to achieve the best results. Experiments confirm that our approach works effectively.

Causal neural learning combines causal inference with neural network technology, with interventional and observational data utilized as inputs. The main causal inference methods include PCAL, which integrates structural equation modeling and directed acyclic graph representation, and potential outcomes framework. Key challenges in this field include regularization of structural causal models from learned representations, handling high-dimensional and complex data through the backdoor path, and efficient exploration of policy and reward spaces in reinforcement learning within causal contexts. This paper provides an in-depth review of causal neural network methodologies and key advancements in this field, including structure learning, variable selection, and reinforcement learning. We also discuss key challenges and potential directions for future research in the area of causal neural network structures.

Understanding how heat moves through gas-solid fluidized beds is crucial for designing many chemical engineering processes that rely on this type of reactor.  A fluidized bed's characteristics, such as its fluid dynamics, can be challenging to study due to the turbulent environment.  To better understand the heat transfer mechanisms at work in these reactors, researchers used rapid MRI technology to monitor the temperature distribution in a gas-fluidized bed in the presence of solid particles.  The MRI technology provided high-resolution 2D temperature maps at a rate of 100 images per second.  Experiments were conducted at different gas velocities without solid particles to study the effects of gas fluctuations on heat transfer.  The findings showed that the temperature fluctuations were significantly reduced when solid particles were added, and a new method was proposed to distinguish between gas and particle-induced temperature changes.  This new method could be applied to study the complex heat transfer processes that occur in fluidized bed reactors.

In the context of algebraic geometry, the "b-principle" usually holds for objects that depend on a sufficient number of parameters within a given family. However, we've recently discovered that for curves, there's an exceptional situation - the number of moduli doesn't grow with the number of available parameters in certain families. M.B. Mumford hypothesized that this exception's scope could be precisely determined. In this research, we've pinpointed the specific families of curves where the dimension of the space of algebraic curves is deficient by exactly one dimension.

Multiple field variables and complex, nonlinear relationships characterize cardiac mechanics, which also includes material and boundary condition changes over time. To model this process effectively, a comprehensive, three-dimensional, user-defined material law-based finite element formulation is required. To overcome these challenges and achieve a realistic simulation, iterative solutions are necessary in both time and space. To facilitate this simulation within a reasonable timeframe, highly efficient multilevel solvers are essential. We examined various multilevel preconditioners, such as algebraic multigrid and Schur complement methods, to determine their effectiveness in cardiac mechanics simulations. We focused on the scalability of these methods across different problem sizes and across multiple computing nodes. To inform the best algebraic multigrid settings, we analyzed the impact of these settings on the solver's performance. To develop realistic simulations, we successfully integrated clinical data and experimentally validated boundary conditions and loading protocols. We examined multilevel preconditioners' scalability with respect to problem size and number of computing nodes to determine their effectiveness in cardiac mechanics simulations.

The well-established connection between random matrix theory and combinatorics involves mapping non-intersecting lattice paths to the probabilities of Hermitian random matrix ensembles. To broaden this link, a study was conducted on an independent and identically distributed unitary random matrix, extending the theory beyond triangular structures. This investigation established a large-N limit for the unitary matrix and demonstrated how its unitary structure influences related Hermitian random matrix distributions. Furthermore, the study derived specific unitary matrix section probabilities, identifying a link with the orthogonal polynomials of the underlying independent entry distributions. These findings were then applied to various hermitian ensembles to reveal how their respective independent entry-based unitary matrix cousins exhibit distinct behaviors.

In recent years, significant advancements have been made in AI-based video creation technology, which includes tasks such as text-to-video and image-to-video. Despite existing surveys on video understanding and still image generation, a comprehensive review of the progress in AI-driven convincing video production has not yet been conducted. This review will cover the advancements in AI-driven convincing video production, including the use of prior knowledge, the replacement of content based on given instructions, and the influence of model scale and computational power on model performance. A key aspect of this review will be to highlight the pressing needs and potential applications of video generation, and to discuss the critical need for objective evaluation metrics, high benchmark standards, and interpretability of models, and these points will be detailed in this review.

We examine the common practice of using contrastive learning to pretrain models before fine-tuning for final applications. While the effectiveness of this approach remains unclear, a prevalent assumption posits that using models in a zero-shot setting following fine-tuning creates a false sense of security. To investigate, we establish a comprehensive benchmark and evaluate the impact of pretraining with contrastive methods on various tasks within the domain of semantic analysis. Our findings indicate that models do preperform in zero-shot scenarios compared to their supervised counterparts, but the primary reason lies in the disparity between distributions rather than a model comprehension issue. Moreover, the advantage of pretraining is limited and primarily observed in domains that are closely related to the one used for pretraining. To address this issue, we propose a simple yet efficient technique called Masked Fine-tuning, which eliminates the need for pretraining while yielding comparable performance gains.

Recently, innovative research has produced remarkable acoustic metagrating devices in the ultrasonic range, overcoming previous limitations associated with high-frequency fabrication. These advanced acoustic metagratings have been developed to counteract unwanted higher-order diffraction effects, which often result in distorted patterns and efficiency losses. Specifically, two novel microacoustic metagrating designs have been fabricated using a cutting-edge fabrication technique known as two-photon lithography, allowing for extremely fine feature sizes. Detailed numerical simulations and experimental measurements demonstrate the effectiveness of these devices in minimizing higher-order diffraction and efficiently directing ultrasonic waves. As a result, one metagrating design successfully directs 92% of 2 MHz sound waves in the forward direction, while another directs 85% of 3 MHz ultrasound in the same direction. This breakthrough research highlights the immense potential of acoustic metagratings and paves the way for highly efficient acoustic devices and systems operating in the ultrasonic frequency range.

In this study, we've analyzed spatially correlated random systems through non-normal diffusion, finding that diffusion's variability grows significantly faster than in any other known configuration, with no equivalent in Hermitian frameworks. By testing our theory on a 2D Gaussian system with covariance defined by the 2D Laplacian, we've discovered both sub- and superdiffusion rates, including a 1.75-dimensional effective diffusion, demonstrating the phenomenon experimentally using fluid flow in fluidization beds.

A straightforward and general model has been developed for describing the linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions in optical resonators and waveguides. This model can be applied to various materials and geometries, including those exhibiting linear or Kerr losses or gain. By utilizing a general approach, the model derives key parameters that define both linear interactions and Kerr effect, such as cross- and phase-kerr coefficients. Furthermore, the model establishes relationships between these parameters and fundamental properties like group velocities, group birefringence, and the Kerr coefficient. Specifically, the model yields a general expression for the normal form of the Hamiltonian, which incorporates group velocity, birefringence, and the Kerr effect. This model is highly versatile and valuable, particularly in the study of weak and strong light-matter interactions.

A key challenge in control systems is ensuring stability and reaching desired states within a set time frame, especially when controls are not limited. This paper builds on previous research to determine stability and control performance using a time-based criterion. These conditions are established through an alternative approach involving the systems' fundamental properties and significant results in differential equations. The proof of these conditions relies on key mathematical theorems, including those related to differential equations and optimal control. An example is provided to illustrate the application of these conditions.

Researchers utilized ultrathin dye streaks to visualize the chaotic mixing within a P\'{e}lton wheel at three varying Reynolds numbers (Re = 1000, 1500, and 2000) and with the bucket rotation speed set at 1000 rpm. A high-speed camera recorded these flows, capturing images at Re = 1000 and 1500 with sufficient resolution, but the recording at Re = 2000 was undersampled. To restore the distorted flow structures, a high-resolution generator network was employed, which successfully restored the flow structures for Re = 2000 using the high-Reynolds number recordings as references. This approach allowed for the transfer of high-resolution details across a range of flow conditions.

For a given region in space, we analyze a specific wave equation related to quantum mechanics. This study focuses on key properties of this analysis and includes examination of various theoretical concepts such as quantum uniqueness, severe limitations, absence of information, and surface limitations.

This study proposes an innovative, user-centric framework for assessing and improving the reliability of learning algorithms in uncharted scenarios. The framework assesses algorithmic confidence by considering both financial incentives and uncertainty, allowing for a more accurate prediction of performance. A key feature of this assessment method is its ability to identify when an untested scenario is significantly different from familiar ones, thus indicating higher levels of uncertainty. In order to improve the reliability of an algorithm's confidence, a new approach is introduced that leverages the ability of learning agents to explore new, untested scenarios. The assessment method is applied to testing the retransfer learning and ambiguity management capabilities of deep neural networks. A unified model is developed to explain the relationship between an algorithm's confidence, levels of ambiguity, and closed- and open-world performance. By using data from untested scenarios, the approach collects a comprehensive dataset that is used to characterize the algorithm and identify ways to enhance its performance. A new strategy is introduced that incentivizes the algorithm to stay within its area of expertise and avoid highly ambiguous situations. The approach is evaluated on a range of learning algorithms, including deep neural networks, across various untested scenarios. The results show that the approach successfully improves the reliability of an algorithm's confidence and allows it to handle a wider range of untested scenarios.

Deep reinforcement learning algorithms have achieved significant success in various applications, but their sample inefficiency poses a major challenge for training on real-world tasks. To overcome this hurdle, simulation environments have become a popular choice for preliminary testing. However, developing simulation models often proves costly and time-consuming. We present the $L_2$ evaluation ecosystem, a groundbreaking framework that accelerates the process of reinforcement learning simulation environment creation. By automating the reward and state space design processes, $L_2$ enables swift prototyping of multiple distinct RL evaluation ecosystems, thus facilitating comparative studies and accelerating innovation in reinforcement learning algorithms.

To enhance process management, monitoring, and analysis in processes that use token-based petri nets, this paper proposes a novel approach by integrating a declarative process model with actual process data. Instead of relying on trace-based process models, which can be inflexible and hinder exploration and analytics in unstructured processes, we suggest monitoring and modeling processes through data flows. Introducing the concept of a process flow, we provide a corresponding formalism and prove its relationship with declarative processes, paving the way for: (a) effective surveillance of processes, (b) conversion of unstructured processes into trace-based models via process projections, and (c) process analytics through flow-based methods. These theories are supported by examples to demonstrate their practical applications.

In one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals formed by coupled waveguide arrays, light propagation can exhibit a sudden transition from being trapped to being free in certain junctions. These 1D structures offer an effective platform for studying quasiperiodic phenomena and associated transverse movement. Our research reveals that in specific Soshnikov sequences, there is a unique occurrence where light goes from being trapped to being free in adjacent sections, which we call reentrant delocalization shifting. This phenomenon is analyzed through numerical simulations and a new mathematical model, providing a clear understanding of when it occurs and demonstrating its rarity due to the coexistence of localized and delocalized states within a single photonic quasicrystal system.

Liger, the high-performance adaptive optics system at the Keck Observatory, is capable of delivering unprecedented sensitivity and resolution in the near-infrared range for both the Keck I and Keck II telescopes, by combining them with superconducting near-infrared cameras. To manage and process the vast amount of data produced by Liger, a robust and efficient processing system has been developed, leveraging the Keck Observatory's computing resources and a range of software tools including Python, IDL, and the Liger Inference Framework. This development stage is nearing completion, and as such, observing with Liger is now possible.

To explore generating high-resolution images, we propose a method to expand the information in each pixel of a binary photon image by analyzing two photons captured at the same time. Our experiment involves sending two photons with specific polarizations and spatial patterns through a setup that records their hit positions on a detector, allowing for a simplified process of image reconstruction based on time-correlated single-photon measurements using a pre-determined filter. By testing this approach, we demonstrate that our bi-photon method achieves superior results compared to standard resolution when recovering an image from a single detection.

The algebraic compactification method known as the Cox ring is being discussed, and the approach is applied to specific geometries, including del Pezzo surfaces and quadrangular tetrahedrons. Additionally, the article introduces a new concept called the algebraic compactification using the Cox ring and demonstrates how the method is utilized to achieve certain results. Furthermore, the author defines the Cox fan and the Cox polytope algebraic compactifications and demonstrates how the approach can be used to specific geometries, including the dp and quadrangular tetrahedrons.

A multi-scale analysis of the ecosystem of birds in the Po Valley, Italy, from 1960 to 2016, revealed early warning signs of sudden shifts in species populations. Researchers used a combination of techniques, including spectral analysis and scaling, to examine the ecosystem and found that it displayed characteristics of both random and predictable behavior. They discovered that some species counts exhibited a chaotic, unpredictable pattern, while others showed predictable cycles. This unpredictable chaos may have served as an early alert system for periods of species population stability and sudden shifts. Specifically, the onset of winter and spring periods was associated with increased chaos in the ecosystem, which was followed by periods of population stability for certain species. Additionally, the decline of the great grey shrike and the recovery of the common starling were made easier to predict by examining the chaotic behavior of the ecosystem. These findings suggest that analyzing the overall, interconnected dynamics of the ecosystem, rather than just individual species, could provide a more effective early alert system for periods of population stability and sudden shifts.

When normalized by star formation rate, the relationship between stellar mass and star formation rate follows a U-shape. Recent studies suggest that structural characteristics, specifically the ratio of bulge to total mass, might be relevant in this context. However, the influence of bulges has not been thoroughly explored in detail. In order to address this knowledge gap, a study was undertaken to map the color-mass-star formation rate relationship while considering different bulge ratios. Utilizing SPARC's comprehensive collection of 13,945 nearby disk galaxies, the study normalized stellar and star formation rates using $M_*^{0.38}$ and $LFIR^{0.19}$, respectively. It was discovered that the specific major axis bulge to total mass ratio ($\mu_b$) holds significant importance in determining a galaxy's color. Furthermore, it was observed that the fundamental plane of star formation exhibits distinct branches that are defined by $\mu_b$. In order to explain this phenomenon, the study proposes that dry and wet mergers, along with major disk instabilities, determine the specific bulge ratio of a galaxy. These processes have the potential to either accelerate or decelerate the specific energy at which gas within a galaxy is converted into stars. Ultimately, $\mu_b$ emerges as the critical factor in determining whether a galaxy is "blue" or "red" and whether it experiences efficient or sluggish star formation.

Emotion recognition and sentiment classification are fundamental techniques for understanding human feelings. They can be seen as a spectrum, with emotion detection being at one end and sentiment classification being at the other. This paper proposes a unified approach to analyzing emotions and classifying sentiments across languages, even without having annotated data for the target language. A multi-task learning framework was devised that involves training two linked classifiers simultaneously: an emotion classifier and a sentiment classifier. This framework was tested on various combinations of languages and tasks, including training and inference on multiple languages. The results indicate that this approach yields superior performance compared to single-language models and basic translation techniques when it comes to annotating emotions in a target language.

We explore the rates of degradation and repair of cooperation in a variant of the Ising model, depicting players' willingness to maintain cooperative behavior after being betrayed. The concept of "fence repair" is modeled after elastic self-force, influencing each player and only activating within a limited range. The dislocation concept is employed to analyze and understand the resulting dynamics. The propagation of cooperative domains is found to be governed by dislocation density, while the repair speed of "bent" fences is relatively high. Notably, low threshold values for disloyalty lead to enhanced cooperative outcomes.

Freiman established the 3k-4 conjecture which posits that any integer subset A with a small number of elements between k and 2k-2 will have a sumset of at least 3k-4 elements. We enhance this by proving a variant where the sumset 22k-4 follows by conditions on 2-base subsets of non-consecutive integers, providing a more rigorous basis for the original 3k-4 conjecture.

Given a Borel measure on R^n that weights density one almost everywhere, the set of functions resembling fractional Brownian motion with unit variance and exponent H in the range (0,1] that minimizes the expected squared norm under this measure is identified. It is proven that if the measure has a finite expected squared norm, then for nearly all such values of fractional Brownian motion in the given variance and exponent range, the set where this minimal value is achieved contains an interior section. Furthermore, if the measure is bounded, then this interior range includes an interval of fractional Brownian motion paths with unit or less amplitude.

A modified Self-Consistent Harmonic Approximation is developed using a quantum test-disorder framework to accurately estimate the ground-state properties of a chaotic system linked with random matrix theory. The approach effectively predicts the lowest energy state and corresponding time-periodic behavior, particularly in relation to H\'enon-Heiles framework that models low-dimensional chaotic dynamics. The framework demonstrates that traditional methods such as harmonic approximation and H\'enon-Heiles framework can be derived from a unified perspective via Dirac's variational principle, resulting in a small discrepancy between predicted and actual results for the system in question.

This paper presents an innovative concept for utilizing digital X-ray images to anticipate which COVID-19 patients will require intensive care. We are searching for specific patterns in CT scans that could serve as indicators of severe disease progression. So far, no method exists for this purpose, making it an area of significant potential development. We propose creating a scoring system based on radiological features to achieve this goal. Furthermore, we aim to investigate the underlying relationships between various features and a patient's clinical status, as well as explore the possibility of leveraging machine learning techniques to enhance predictive capabilities.

We establish that a simplicial bundle's total space comprises a simplicial structure, making the bundle classification possible via an adapted Cartan-Gauss theorem. This achievement is accomplished by adapting the Dold's method for converting simplicial complexes to CW-complexes, with our result being a generalization of Dold's theorem for covering maps.

A recent problem in detecting objects within videos is the occurrence of false associations between objects and actions due to high data density in annotated action localization datasets, resulting in missed detections and associations with unrelated objects. To address this issue, we propose a novel strategy to create balanced sampling subsets that cover various scenarios from clear false associations to instances of irrelevant background objects. This approach allows researchers to specifically focus on improving the evaluation and modeling of action relationships. By evaluating both carefully designed baseline models and more advanced methods using our balanced subsets, we observed that current evaluation standards heavily favor models based on global information and temporal context, leading to false associations. In response, we developed a novel framework that combines carefully designed super-graphs for action relationships with BERT-based processing to accurately handle action associations. Our experiments show that this multi-stage relationship-aware model significantly improves the evaluation of action relationships, achieving a notable reduction in weighted misclassification error rate compared to the initial model.

This study proposes an action recognition model called DSR-BERT, which is based on a pre-trained BERT architecture and is suitable for action recognition tasks that are constrained by limited data or low-light conditions. One advantage of using the BERT framework is its capability to effectively handle partially labeled data through a cross-entropy loss function, and BERT's attention mechanism allows it to pinpoint key frames that contain essential information for action recognition. To address action recognition tasks that are constrained, this study introduces a delta sampling method that reduces the number of video frames that need to be processed, and simultaneously increases the model's capacity to extract information from images. Experiments conducted on the NTU-RGB+D dataset show that the DSR-BERT model achieves a top-1 accuracy of 81.9%, outperforming other transformer-based models by 1.3%.

This research proposes a novel Content-Addressable Parallel Processing architecture, combining elements of Content Addressable Memory and SIMD. We developed an FPGA prototype for efficient data management, featuring simultaneous search and processing capabilities. By integrating CAM and SIMD, our Content-Addressable Concurrent Processors (CACP) reduce the need for repetitive instructions and enhance performance through parallel operations on linked memory. We demonstrated significant performance improvements through benchmarking, comparing CACP with traditional SIMD implementations and observing up to a ten-fold increase in performance and a substantial reduction in power consumption.

At high redshift, galaxy mergers are generally considered a key factor in the rapid growth of galaxies. However, a significant number of galaxy formations observed outside of major mergers are still unaccounted for. We studied 16 external disk galaxies located within a cluster at redshift 3 in a process that is often characterized by relative stability. Discoveries were made of significant differences in color across two of these galaxies, indicating possible major galaxy formations outside of the central regions. By analyzing near-infrared light, we observed that the inner regions of these galaxies are developing bulges faster than their outer regions. By estimating the rate of star formation and applying a model for energy transfer, we found that the inner regions are likely experiencing a more intense galaxy formation process, which is causing bulge development, while the rest of the galaxy is forming bulges as a result of a less intense galaxy formation process. These findings suggest that galaxy formation processes can cause bulge development on their own, which is likely applicable to a significant number of 1 galaxies located at high redshifts.

In the context of flavor physics, a global texture zero hypothesis is a widely studied theory that posits the existence of zero entries in the flavor matrices. This examination employs a rigorous statistical approach using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to reassess the viability of this hypothesis. By incorporating recent experimental data from neutrino and lepton flavor mixing, researchers conducted multiple MCMC simulations to evaluate the probability of the global texture zero hypothesis being true. However, despite these rigorous examinations, a statistically significant result could not be obtained, suggesting that more constraints may be necessary to validate this theoretical framework.

This study introduces a new approach to analyze the behavior of solutions to a specific type of elliptic equation, specifically those involving bubbling. For a given domain in n-dimensional space, we examine the number of solutions that exhibit bubbling as a parameter increases, by applying a bisection method based on an index function. This method enables us to determine the number of distinct solutions that exhibit bubbling by calculating the index at points where solutions cease to exist. Our results show that for certain types of domains, particularly star-shaped ones, there must be solutions that exhibit bubbling with a specific pattern of symmetry.

Although the static analysis of programs offers valuable insights, it frequently suffers from imprecise results. This limitation can be seen as a beneficial aspect, as it can be leveraged in programs' creation. We investigate the use of imperfect static evaluation in generating high-quality synthetic data for training and evaluating programs, specifically for the Counter example Generation (CEG) and Filling (CF) problems. By examining four different evaluation strategies, we develop systems that employ Counter Based Learning (CBL) to create counter examples and programs to fix issues identified by the evaluators. Our experiments, conducted with random Counter Based Learning (CBL) as a baseline, demonstrate that incorporating static evaluation in generating training data for CBL significantly enhances its performance in solving CEG and CF problems. Moreover, we find that more effective synthetic data can be produced when counter examples and programs are evaluated on multiple inputs rather than just one.

On November 4-5, 2004, a solar neutron event was detected in Japan, with data collected by J-PARC's neutron monitor. Analysis of this event revealed that existing background models were inaccurate, prompting a revised decomposition algorithm. This new algorithm accounted for the observed solar neutron event correctly and accurately represented data points in a specific energy range. Furthermore, it was discovered that the existing J-PARC background algorithm underestimates the actual background levels.

We derive the propagation relations for small fluctuations in a relativistic, four-dimensional, viscous fluid at equilibrium. Our derivation is based on using the covariant decomposition of the acceleration, antisymmetric tensor, and four-velocity. We establish that there are thirteen distinct modes of propagation, including two transverse modes of shear, two bulk modes, two sound modes, and additionally, four entropic modes, a mode of gravitational type, and a mode of mixed nature, all occurring within the fluid's equatorial plane perpendicular to the fluid's overall movement.

One-shot anomaly detection techniques struggle to identify subtle changes in sensor readings due to their high level of robustness. To counter this, we developed InQMAD, an innovative measurement irregularity detection method that utilizes a quantization-based neural network framework. InQMAD gradually adds hidden layers to its network to detect and accommodate measurement irregularities incrementally. This design allows it to detect subtle shifts in data without compromising its security, making it well-suited for use in secure systems that rely on cryptographic authentication.

This research proposes a method for an adversary to validate whether an authorized third party is capable of accessing encrypted data held by the data owner. We develop a Method of Forced Confirmation (MFC) allowing the adversary to verify properties of the encrypted data without revealing it. Specifically, we demonstrate that an attacker can confirm mathematical operations being performed on Homomorphic Encryption (HE) data. We analyze various HE schemes, including Paillier, BN, BGV, and CKKS. Through confirmable transformations, the attacker can confirm whether the authorized third party has obtained access to the encrypted data. We define the security framework for confirmation-transformable HE (CTHE) and provide a security proof for MFC. Our analysis covers multiple scenarios, including confirming encrypted images, numerical data, and Chinese characters. Furthermore, real-world experiments show that the proposed method is both feasible and efficient.

We have developed a universal framework for simulating the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process, which is adaptable to various simulation scenarios. This framework allows for the flexible experimentation of different quantum states and the assessment of real-world MZI setups and measurement devices using actual QKD hardware. In addition, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model by accurately predicting the observed gain and secure key rate in both a 100-km fiber simulation and a real-world MDI-QKD field test. The framework is further applicable to other measurement-device-independent quantum communication protocols.

For a specific type of constraint satisfaction problem, we're looking at instances where constraints are organized in a sparse structure, characterized by a constraint graph that has a limited number of constraints at each node. This analysis applies to various weighted CSP problems, including those with organization constraints and numerical constraints like minimum spanning tree and directed multi-terminal cut. When the constraint graph has a certain level of sparseness, defined by a bound $\tau$, we can solve these CSP problems with an approximate cost that's very close to the optimal solution. Specifically, for any desired level of sparseness $\tau$ and any $\varepsilon$ greater than zero, we have a polynomial-time method to solve these CSP problems with a cost within a factor of $O(\tau^{1/\varepsilon})$ of the optimal. This result represents a notable improvement, providing an efficient approximation method where previously only constant or exponential approximations were feasible.

This research focuses on a specific type of Fokker-Planck equation, particularly one associated with mean field games. We've been investigating a novel numerical approach, combining Lagrange-Galerkin methods, for this equation. This approach enables us to handle the velocity field within the equation in a more natural way. We've proven that for a decreasing time step, this method yields an consistent result, providing an error bound of $h^{k+1}$, where $h$ denotes the mesh size and $k$ denotes the polynomial degree of the basis functions.

This project focuses on the operability, comprehension, and representation of neural networks through the use of generative models, specifically Variational Auto-Encoders (VAEs). We have employed cutting-edge techniques to analyze and interpret both Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). Our study encompasses three key aspects of using VAEs to interpret neural networks: (i) re-generating input data that aligns with a given class, (ii) producing class-specific visual concepts, and (3) creating interpretable class-specific code. We have applied these methods to interpret both a ResNet-50 on the ImageNet dataset and a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory network on the Twitter sentiment analysis dataset. Our results have demonstrated that VAEs can effectively capture the operational principles of neural networks with high accuracy. Moreover, we have developed a novel approach to evaluate the comprehension and comprehension representativeness of neural networks by leveraging the ability of generative models.

Recent observations of a nearby star, L 99-8, have revealed a surprising amount of spin in it. In contrast, standard models of stellar development predict that it should still be relatively slow due to its youth. L 99-8 is already known to host at least one planet, possibly more, which may play a role in this unexpected amount of spin. We conducted an in-depth analysis of L 99-8's properties and found that the angular momentum transfer from the planets could be responsible for its higher levels of rotation. We explored various scenarios and found that tidal interactions between the star and the planets could be transferred in a way that accounts for the observed levels of rotation. We estimate that the innermost planet has already experienced some damage, and there is a possibility that it could be swallowed by the star. We also performed additional simulations of a single planet scenario and found that they support our initial findings.

Multimodal news articles that combine text and images are frequently shared on social media, but there's a growing problem with deceptive content that's hard to detect due to only one authentic modality being available.  To address this issue, we propose a novel unsupervised learning framework called MetaCNN, a meta-learning approach that processes multimodal news articles and effectively identifies counterfeit content.  By drawing on established principles from meta-learning and neural processing, MetaCNN enables the model to acquire a versatile decision-making capability, allowing it to identify counterfeit content in various types of news articles, including those with fake images or manipulated text.  Experimental results on a newly created dataset show that MetaCNN outperforms existing unsupervised learning methods for detecting multimodal news authenticity by a significant margin of 8.1%.

This research focuses on the properties of a specific type of partial differential equation known as the degenerate transport equation, particularly in situations where there's a periodic recurring pattern. It also examines the implications of this recurring behavior on solutions to related equations. A key innovation in the study is the development of a novel verification method for solutions, which is then applied to prove the existence of unique periodic solutions under broader conditions of data regularity.

Research on age-based decision-making in condition monitoring has gained significant attention in recent years. This work introduces an age-based replacement framework for discrete time systems that closely relates to the literature on age-based interventions in conditioning. A mathematical model is established to calculate the long-term average cost within this Discrete Time system. The minimization of cost is analyzed and the properties of its optimal solution are explored in detail. A novel algorithm is proposed to efficiently determine the parameter values that minimize cost. This research is theoretically supported by proofs and practical insights illustrated through numerical examples. Key disconditions identified within this model include those related to cost constraints, and the characteristics of cost-controlling parameters are examined across various scenarios. The proposed algorithm is validated and its performance assessed through simulation. A unique approach is introduced to address issues of feasible solution constraints within the algorithm. Finally, the connection between the Ber/G/1/1 queue and the discrete time condition monitoring system is discussed, highlighting the broader implications and potential applications of this work.

Solving the quantum group deformation of the R-matrix associated with the quantum algebra leads to new structures, such as quasi-bialgebras. This paper investigates the deformation of the R-matrix by studying the set of its $\delta$-solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. By analyzing various aspects of these solutions, including their multiplicativity, interaction with the R-matrix cross-over property, and their parametric variations, a specific set of matrices is obtained. This set defines new constants that characterize the resulting quasi-bialgebra structure, including its associator.

Recently, Golay complementary structures (GCS) have gained significant interest due to their unique properties that can be rescaled and shifted with ease, making them suitable for modern filtering technologies, particularly in multichannel systems. Although research on integer-based GCS has made considerable progress in recent years, very little is known about complex-valued GCS, especially in multichannel setups. This study introduces the concept of complex GCS (CGCS) and develops several CGCS construction techniques that can be adapted for multichannel coherent filtering applications. Specifically, we have developed four novel CGCS construction techniques in Year N, including two new methods combining Hadamard and Fourier matrices, as well as Complementary Binary Structures (CBS). To demonstrate the effectiveness of these techniques, we have constructed several CGCS with specific parameters and element sets in years 7, 8, 9, and 10.

A theoretical analysis of valley interaction and spin transfer in a molecular silicon setup is presented. It is found that valley coupling between two methyl-terminated ethyl groups leads to an interplay of spin and valley phenomena, resulting in valley-mediated inter-molecular valley polar transfer. Notably, this setting may allow for the development of silicon-based quantum devices that exploit both valley and spin characteristics.

Machine Learning methods have been effectively applied to study intricate systems such as economies and complex networks, yet a significant limitation exists in these models: the white-box nature is lacking, hindering an in-depth understanding of the interplay between model structure and system dynamics. This issue becomes particularly acute when conducting experiments aimed at manipulating the dynamics and subsequently predicting the resulting effects. This research presents a novel graph neural network framework that allows for the examination of the connection between model architecture and system dynamics by presenting a cutting-edge approach that integrates a historical graph representation method with a learning process based on graph neural network techniques. This innovative method enables an examination of how different model structures influence the model's learning capabilities and representation efficiency. We applied this method to analyze market phenomena, exploring how different model topologies and information-sharing mechanisms impact market efficiency. We also conducted experiments on Integrated Learning over Networks (ILoN) to investigate how different graph structures impact both sample efficiency and performance. We also discovered that the chosen structure significantly impacts the efficiency with which the model can be trained and its performance. We also conducted additional experiments to verify the interpretability of the learned representations. We also presented our model as an innovative tool for researchers to explore the impact of architectural choices on learning processes in machine models.

We develop a concept of directed partitions that enables us to establish an order within the homotopy category of 1-categorical presentable stable $\infty$-categories, specifically those with exact functors that preserve all small colimits. This development builds upon the foundation laid by Nopstein's original idea, which has found a stable counterpart in the context of $\infty$-categories. These advancements allow us to establish the equivalence of the homotopy categories of directed (or stable directed) partitions with the classification $\mathcal{F}at_\mathcal{C}$ (or $\mathcal{Fat}^0_\mathcal{C}$) of exact functors from a given presentable stable $\infty$-category $\mathcal{C}$ and all its power iterations to the stable $\infty$-category of presentable categories with exact functors that preserve all small colimits.

Certain neurological disorders, including cerebral lesions, can cause significant impairment or even death. Accurately predicting these pathologies is a complex task, and deep learning models require a large number of annotated real-life images for effective training. To overcome data limitations, researchers are developing synthetic lesion datasets to supplement their studies. However, current methods for generating multiple lesions in a single image are often unrealistic and easily identified as fake by validation networks. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called the Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder, which can be applied to both single and multi-lesion generation in mouse brain images. By gradually increasing the number of generated lesions through a two-phase process, our method ensures better realism and coherence in the resulting images. We also introduce a lesions similarity loss function to prevent superposition and improve the quality of generated lesions. Our approach outperforms existing techniques in terms of realism, coherence, and efficiency, and is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenZ1999/PAL.

The nonlocal nature of quantum mechanics is best demonstrated by the violation of inequalities of Bell, however, the necessary conditions of measurement and state purity for such violations are best achieved with maximal entangled states. Not all states with entanglement can fulfill the inequality of Bell effectively, and in this research, we identify robust quantum nonlocality in robust entanglement for unextendable product states through randomized measurements and robust Robust Irdentifiable Nonlocality (IRNL) values. These measurements and IRNL values are robust to noise and can be measured reliably.

We experimentally validate the secure coordination algorithm for robotic teams developed by our previous research. Using an astrobot simulation, we evaluated the algorithm's effectiveness in real-world applications, specifically in verifying data accuracy for the fifth data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. This involved evaluating the algorithm's ability to maintain thorough coordination among robots and assess its efficiency. Our results demonstrate that the algorithm can accurately gather data through thorough coordination among astrobots. Although there are some discrepancies between our astrobot experiments and optimal collection times used by other researchers, our algorithm successfully achieves the goal of accurate, coordinated data collection.

Building a high-level description language for research purposes, GP 2, allows for rapid development and easy reconfiguration of systems. It has a distinguishing feature of an advanced compiler that uses a graph-based technique to enhance system performance. By analyzing and transforming the code, the compiler identifies areas for optimization and applies specific strategies to improve efficiency. Over the past ten years, research has focused on developing new components and technologies. This paper reviews these advancements and highlights specific examples, while also exploring potential areas for further growth in GP 2.

To improve information extraction from news, we have developed a unified structure that incorporates various formats and focuses on attribute extraction using contrastive learning. This model, which utilizes BERT and a unique matrix to handle different document structures, extracts short-term information from each section of a news item. Through the application of contrastive learning, we guide a hidden layer to identify a unified space where similar information is closely related. To fine-tune the initial extraction, we employ a classification layer to optimize the distance between the extracted information and its target. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that this model achieves a high level of accuracy and efficiency in extracting key attributes from diverse types of news.

A directed graph is considered a star normal quotient network (SNQN) of a group if, for any two of its edges, the corresponding core edges belong to a specific normal subgroup. In this context, we investigate the SNQNs of a particular class of groups known as twisted wreath groups. We provide the core edges for a collection of directed graphs that are of twisted wreath type, and it is shown that these graphs are indeed SNQNs. Our findings contribute to the broader field by expanding the collection of SNQNs for finite groups.

For the selective removal of irrelevant information as we scale, hierarchical categorical models have been widely used for feature selection and cluster analysis.  Despite their effectiveness, working with large-scale hierarchical structures becomes computationally challenging due to the significant increase in model parameters and complex connections.  To address this issue for high-dimensional data, a Group Lasso extension of the hierarchical structures is proposed.  By extending the penalty to subspaces defined by the hierarchy, this extension allows for more efficient sparse solutions.  A specific algorithm is proposed to solve the proposed model, and both simulation studies and real-world data analyses demonstrate its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy, model sparsity, and recovery of underlying hierarchy-relevant structures when noise levels are high.

Deep neural network models have achieved remarkable performance in vision tasks,
yet they remain susceptible to subtle manipulations that humans can easily detect.
Expert annotations are frequently required to compensate for the limited insight
that deep models possess. We propose a novel approach called SKILL, which infuses
structured knowledge into large language models to generate detailed explanations
and insights about image contents. We evaluated the impact of infused knowledge on
large language models by employing diverse queries and utilizing expert annotations
as a benchmark. Our results indicate that the explanation quality can be significantly
improved by infusing knowledge, whereas generic prompts fail to produce detailed
insights. We made SKILL open-source to facilitate further research into explaining
and enhancing neural models at https://github.com/cis-tron/SKILL.

This research introduces a nonlocal diffusion model based on a grid of points in space, defined over a specific range. It examines the model's behavior as the distance between points decreases, ultimately converging to a local diffusion model as indicated by a density function. The research also examines a second, distinct convergence scenario, resulting in a coherent fractional diffusion equation. Both limits are ultimately achieved through the manipulation of two key variables: the interaction range and the density between points interacting.

Traditional panoramic techniques rely on aligning images based on their content, which can be influenced by the direction images are oriented in, particularly the preference for gravity. This preference can improve the efficiency of panoramic stitching by utilizing pre-aligned images that have been oriented according to the direction they face, rather than relying on feature matching. A method suggested involves using a single feature, such as a vanishing point or horizon, to link and stitch together these pre-aligned images into a panorama. We investigated a method to connect these features that varies in complexity, and discovered that doing so by equating a specific parameter, such as the horizon's position, results in noticeable distortions. We also found that incorporating an additional feature, such as a vanishing line, can improve the stitching process.

The paper provides a fresh approach to resolving an open problem from Piatetski-Shapiro, by offering a new strategy to demonstrate the elimination of pole residues for a specific sum involving Eisenstein series. The article aims to achieve this by presenting an alternative method to proving the desired outcome for the given sum. Furthermore, the proposed method can be applied to other summation scenarios and potentially leads to advancements in the understanding of the Plancherel measure for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$.

Neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's, significantly impact human life worldwide. As a result, researchers are committed to developing effective computational models to analyze these conditions. However, existing computational models have limitations, such as an over-reliance on mouse-based data and a lack of integration of biophysical aspects. In response, we propose a novel computational framework that utilizes a biophysical approach, based on gene expression data from healthy and Parkinson's-affected brain samples of marmoset monkeys. This model is created using a multi-objective optimization technique called genetic algorithm. By employing this innovative model, we can better understand the complex interactions between genes and, ultimately, develop more targeted treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.

Recently, line-based connections on digital maps have gained significant popularity due to their unique navigational capabilities that only AI technology can achieve. However, as map features grow in complexity, the underlying data structures, which are typically organized by tiles, can hinder processing efficiency. This limitation restricts line connections from operating effectively across large areas. To overcome this challenge, our research proposes a novel approach that enables efficient and seamless line connections over connected map tiles. Our method involves converting the digital map into a grid format, which allows for optimized line connections and can also be applied to other line-navigation applications that rely on maps.

Our research focuses on 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close by, which have high central densities. We used the KOOLS-IFU on the Seimei Telescope to observe these distant celestial bodies, which are situated between 0.005 and 0.038 billion light years away. We detected 200 infrared sources in the observed spectral ranges of 0.58 to 0.89 micrometers, which provided us with redshift values. We found that the rest of the sample's redshift values are between 0.005 and 0.038 billion light years. We derived oxygen abundances from the observed spectral lines and found that the average oxygen abundances in these galaxies are 8.35 +/- 0.18, which are 0.18 +/- 0.15 lower than in a similar population of very luminous infrared galaxies. We found that oxygen abundances are correlated with another measure called specific star formation rate, which indicates that the more active a galaxy is in star formation, the more enriched it is in oxygen. We also observed that the oxygen abundances are correlated with another measure called absolute K-band magnitude, which indicates that brighter galaxies are more enriched in oxygen. We found that the oxygen abundances are correlated with another measure called star formation rate derived from the cooling of hydrogen, which are consistent with our previous observations. This paper introduces a new interpolation method utilizing the hyperbolic tangent function as a basis, resulting in an interpolation operator that maintains linear accuracy and preserves convexity, and also has a smooth derivative, like the convexity and other high-order properties. Furthermore, numerical experiments validate the efficiency of the proposed interpolation scheme, and show that increasing the shape parameter yields better approximation results.

This research paper introduces an innovative concept called Climate Categorization, which utilizes image-based deep learning to automatically classify the climate of any given location. To date, no studies have explored this problem, prompting the creation of a unique dataset encompassing 10 diverse climate types across 90 locations worldwide. To address the issue of dataset imbalance, a new data augmentation technique is proposed, leveraging graph convolutional neural networks to analyze and propagate climate information between visually similar but climatically unrelated locations. Several established image classification models are evaluated on this groundbreaking dataset, revealing that even the best-performing approach achieved below 90% accuracy. Notably, the proposed data augmentation technique surpassed all alternatives, yet there remains significant scope for enhancement. This discovery yields a high-quality, annotated dataset of 10 climate classes, accessible to the research community.

To restore the speech quality of recordings that have been artificially enhanced, a noise model is typically used to predict and remove noise. However, this approach is limited by the need to model speech and noise interactions, as well as the variability of real-world noisy data. In this paper, we propose a novel end-to-end neural network called the Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network, which combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural network models. This allows for more accurate speech estimation and temporal context utilization. Experiments conducted on telephone speech show that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of mean squared error, correlation, and objective speech intelligibility.

Using a non-equilibrium approach, we've explored how modified gravity and neutrino physics can influence the growth of dark matter structures. Specifically, we applied our method to determine the turn-around radii of these formations at various redshifts. We've assessed the individual and combined impacts of an $R^2$ gravity theory and neutrinos with high masses on their sizes. Our research reveals that the expansion rate of the universe's background affects the growth of dark matter structures through its Hamilton-Jacobi equation. The choice of gravity theory influences both the apparent acceleration due to gravity and the gravitational potential well. The mass of heavy neutrinos has an impact on the size of these formations, with the effect being more pronounced for lighter neutrinos. The result can be summarized as follows: the turn-around radius at a given redshift is directly related to the square root of the ratio of a modified gravitational constant and the actual mass of the neutrinos.

This study aims to develop a multi-fluid model for atmospheric circulation by first calibrating a basic model with two fluids under Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection conditions. We adapt the fundamental equations of fluid dynamics, incorporating radiative transfer, for each fluid individually and apply them to a single-column model. There are several approaches to developing a two-fluid system, where interfaces can be passive surfaces or actively influenced by factors such as density differences. We focus on the latter approach, where the interface is described using the Navier-Stokes-Keldysh equation. We compare our results with established two-fluid convection models and discuss how to extend this research to multi-layer atmospheric models.

We examine a system of isolated two-level atoms that do not interact with each other but are linked to common cavity fields in the Jaynes-Cummings model. Based on criteria for entanglement, we investigate whether any quantum state without classical correlations can exist in this system and find that entangled states are not possible in certain cases. In a specific scenario where the cavity fields are among Fock states, we prove that any state with no classical correlations is entangled. In the broader context, entangled states are also not possible except for a very limited set of states. Interestingly, we find that entanglement can exist only for a finite duration in all possible states of this system. Numerical analysis indicates that larger systems are entangled for longer periods. Entanglement duration is found to be significantly affected by the system's energy. Entanglement exists most efficiently in adjacent energy levels.

Approximately 50,000 silicon pixel detectors will be installed in the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider following its upgrade, which are critical for identifying high momentum particles entering the interaction point and reconstructing complex tracks from scattered particles. The current set of sensors, known as triple modules, consist of three layers of detectors separated by 4cm, however, as luminosity increases, they may struggle to record and recover tracks due to temporary sensor damage from laser testing. The proposed single-module design with a larger surface and reduced layer spacing of 2cm is being evaluated as an alternative, and a detailed simulation of their performance was conducted to verify their feasibility. The simulation results demonstrate that the new design successfully recovers over 90% of tracks in certain conditions, verifying its viability. The examination of data processing and track recovery was conducted to verify its feasibility. The results were verified by a detailed simulation of the sensors' performance. The current design successfully recovers over 90% of tracks in certain conditions, however, track fitting accuracy was found to be lower. The current set of sensors will struggle to record and recover tracks due to temporary sensor damage from laser testing, however, the new design is feasible and performs well in certain conditions. Using a Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral depiction approach, we have identified the Kall\'en-Lehmann weights for the SU(2) glueball in scalar channels, specifically looking for the lightest scalar state. By applying the LQCD spectral equation method, we obtained these weights and discovered that the glueball appears in the first step as a single pole, with a mass of 2.94(6)(6) GeV. This finding is in line with recent studies and appears to be the most reliable prediction for the glueball mass to date.

Social sentiment analysis is a vital step in understanding and managing public opinion on various important topics. To accurately determine public opinion, it is essential to analyze the sentiment expressed in people's opinions, which can be effectively done using advanced natural language processing techniques. This study presents a novel multi-task learning approach based on Long Short-Term Memory networks for determining the sentiment expressed in social media posts. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, achieving top-tier performance on benchmark datasets.

To linear order in the graviton's mass, a massless Kerr-Newman-AdS black hole exhibits a significantly larger horizon area for its shadow compared to a non-rotating counterpart. The phenomenon of shadow casting is intimately tied to the geodesic paths of photons, which are affected by both the spin and electric charge of a black hole, ultimately altering the size and shape of the shadow cast. Analyzing the thermodynamic properties encoded within black hole shadows reveals that, in the high-temperature regime, shadow-based entropy and free energy calculations yield the same results as traditional methods, whereas in low-temperature scenarios, shadow-derived calculations diverge from their non-rotating equivalents due to the influence of the black hole's angular momentum on photon trajectories, ultimately altering the shadow's characteristics.

This research focuses on identifying quantum correlations in quantum tomograms and comparing it to a previously established measure. We apply the entanglement criteria to various tomograms, including mixed states, entangled states, superposed states, and non-separable states. Notably, we observed a previously unreported phenomenon of synchronization between local tomograms in entangled states. We also explore potential applications of our method in entangled multi-partite states and quantum fields. A key advantage of our approach is its non-contextual nature. We demonstrate the method's efficacy by examining the entanglement in Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states and symmetric states, showing tomograms' capacity to reveal the extent of correlations. We propose calling this finding "quantum synchronization," a term that can be applied in broader contexts.

We introduce a novel framework, Role-Convex, for creating a conversation framework that leverages language models with access to external knowledge. This framework enables the generation of dialogue that takes into account external knowledge, the utilization of diverse roles, and external world knowledge. By integrating a comprehensive set of tools that includes a role-assigned distribution, conversation management strategies, and an efficient method for selecting models, we ensure that the language model improves while remaining consistent with the defined roles. The Role-Convex framework is designed to be extensible and adaptable to various roles and domains. Experimentation with the role-assigned distribution on multiple scales of external knowledge demonstrates that the proposed framework results in dialogue that is engaging, adheres to the defined roles, and effectively utilizes external knowledge. The Role-Convex framework is available for public use at https://github.com/asthatsky/Role-Defined-Open-Domain-Conversation-Framework.

Evaluating the effectiveness of systems against pests, like preventing strawberries from getting infected, is a challenging problem that can be solved more accurately using a "strong method" in decision analysis. This paper demonstrates how using a strong method, specifically the multiattribute decision-making approach, can assess the efficacy of various pest control methods for preventing strawberry infections. By comparing this approach to traditional techniques, we show that there are advantages to utilizing a strong method in tackling this issue.

360-degree video is a cutting-edge technology that provides an immersive experience, but suffers from large file sizes and low playback efficiency on mobile devices. Research is focused on developing techniques to optimize these videos, specifically through viewport prediction which limits video transmission to areas within a dynamic playback viewport. However, current methods ignore the availability of video subtitles that provide key information about the scene. This paper proposes a new approach to predicting viewports in videos with subtitles by selectively applying subtitle information for areas within the playback viewport. This new framework combines subtitle information with deep learning to accurately predict viewports, resulting in efficient mobile playback. Our deep learning model takes into account the play orientation and the content within the video, leading to a more accurate viewport prediction. This new framework is called Subtitle-driven Viewport Forecasting and includes two optimized versions that focus on different areas of the video. Our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, reducing data transmission requirements and improving playback efficiency.
